title: When gradients vanish
objectives: Explain why saturating activations and deep products of small slopes make gradients vanish.

screens.title: Which layer learns?
screens.prose: A net of ten sigmoid layers, each 100 wide, starts from weights with sd 0.1. One backward pass on a batch of 64 gives each layer's weights a gradient. The bars show their sizes on a log scale.

params.xLabel: Layer (1 is next to the input)

state.caption: Ten sigmoid layers of width 100, weights with sd 0.1, one batch of 64.

screens.question: With one step size for every layer, which layer's weights move the most?

options.text: Layer 1, next to the input, since everything flows through it
options.why: Everything flows through it, but its gradient is the smallest: about 4.4e-08.

options.text: All about the same: the layers are the same size
options.why: The bars span from 4.4e-08 to 0.12, a factor of millions.

options.text: A middle layer, where signal and gradient balance
options.why: The bars fall steadily from the output back to the input.

hints.text: A step moves each weight by the step size times its gradient.
Compare the tallest and shortest bars.

feedback.correct: Layer 10: its gradient is 0.123, against 4.4e-08 for layer 1, about 2.8 million times smaller.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the bars from right to left.

byKey.first: That is the trap of the picture: layer 1 matters most to the output, yet gets the weakest signal.

explain.text: Each layer back from the output shrinks the gradient by roughly a factor of 4 to 5, so layer 1 gets 4.4e-08 against 0.123. With one step size, the early layers barely move.

screens.title: A product of slopes
screens.prose: Name it: the backward pass multiplies by each layer's **activation slope**. The sigmoid's slope $\sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))$ is at most 0.25, at $z = 0$. So a gradient that crosses ten sigmoid layers is multiplied by at most $0.25^{10}$ from the slopes alone: it **vanishes**.
screens.question: What is $0.25^{10}$? Give it in units of $10^{-7}$, to 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply 0.25 by itself ten times.

byKey.linear: You multiplied 0.25 by 10. The slopes multiply, so it is a power.

explain.text: Ten factors of at most 0.25 give at most $9.5 \times 10^{-7}$. The weights add factors of their own, but the slopes alone make the gradient vanish.

screens.title: Reading the slopes
screens.prose: The curves are the slopes of the sigmoid and of tanh. Slide the input. A tanh unit with input 3 is **saturated**: it sits on the flat part, where the slope is nearly 0.

derive.caption: $z$ = {{fixed(z, 1)}}: sigmoid slope {{fixed(exp(-z) / pow(1 + exp(-z), 2), 4)}}, tanh slope {{fixed(1 - pow((exp(z) - exp(-z)) / (exp(z) + exp(-z)), 2), 4)}}

screens.question: What is the tanh slope $1 - \tanh^2(3)$ at an input of 3? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Read the tanh slope in the caption.

feedback.correct: $1 - \tanh^2(3) = 0.0099$: a gradient through that unit keeps under 1% of itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the tanh curve at 3.

byKey.sig: That is the sigmoid's slope at 3.
byKey.notsq: You took $1 - \tanh(3)$; the slope squares the tanh.

explain.text: At $z = 3$ tanh is 0.9951, so its slope is 0.0099. tanh's slope peaks at 1 at $z = 0$, four times the sigmoid's peak, and both die away for large $|z|$.

screens.title: Down one path
screens.prose: One path runs down four sigmoid layers with every weight on it equal to 1. The table gives each layer's pre-activation and slope.

state.caption: One path down four sigmoid layers, every weight on it equal to 1.

screens.question: What factor do the four slopes apply to a gradient on this path? Give 4 significant figures.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The backward pass multiplies the slopes.

byKey.sum: You added the slopes. The chain rule multiplies them.
byKey.peak: That is $0.25^4$, every unit at its steepest; these are flatter.

explain.text: The product is 0.001213: four ordinary pre-activations cost a factor of about 800. Saturated units cost far more.

screens.title: Dead units
screens.prose: ReLU's slope is 1 for $z > 0$ and 0 otherwise, so it never shrinks a passing gradient. But a unit whose pre-activation is never positive on the data passes nothing back: a **dead** unit, which no step can revive.

state.caption: A ReLU layer after training. Slope 0 at $z \le 0$, as in our autograd.

screens.question: How many of these six units are dead on these 200 rows?

hints.text: A unit lives if its largest pre-activation is above 0.
Unit 6 peaks at exactly 0, where the slope is 0.

feedback.correct: Three: units 2, 4 and 6 never get a positive pre-activation, so their slope is 0 on every row.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count units whose largest pre-activation is at most 0.

byKey.neg: Unit 6 peaks at exactly 0, and the slope there is 0, so it is dead too.
byKey.small: Unit 3 peaks at 0.05, above 0, so it still passes gradient on some rows.

explain.text: Units 2, 4 and 6 have slope 0 on every row, so their weights get no gradient and stay dead. Unit 3, at 0.05, is alive on at least one row.

screens.title: Overfitting, or failing to fit?
screens.prose: Dev trains the ten-layer sigmoid net on 400 points. After 300 steps the training loss has hardly moved from where it started. He decides the net is too big and must be overfitting.
screens.question: What is the better diagnosis?

options.text: It cannot fit the training data: gradients vanish
Overfitting: a big net memorises noise
options.why: Overfitting needs a low training loss and a high held-out one; here even the training loss is stuck.

options.text: Too little data: 400 points cannot train ten layers
options.why: More data would not help a net whose early layers barely move on the data it has.

options.text: The step size is too large
options.why: A large step makes the loss jump or blow up; this loss barely moves.

hints.text: Overfitting means low training loss and high held-out loss.
Here the training loss is stuck: the net cannot fit.

feedback.correct: Failing to fit: the training loss is stuck because the early layers' gradients have vanished.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at the training loss first.

byKey.overfit: That is the misconception: a deep sigmoid net often fails on the training data itself, which overfitting cannot explain.

explain.text: Overfitting shows a training loss far below the held-out loss. A training loss that will not fall points to optimisation: here the slopes of ten sigmoid layers.

screens.title: Income in pounds
screens.prose: A credit model feeds raw annual income in pounds into a tanh unit beside ratios that sit near 1. With a weight of 0.0001, an income of £52,000 gives a pre-activation of 5.2.
screens.question: What is the unit's slope there? Give it in units of $10^{-4}$, to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $1 - \tanh^2(5.2) = 1.22 \times 10^{-4}$: the unit is saturated, so its weights barely learn. Standardised (`stat-learning` l9), the same customer gives about $z = 0.3$ and a slope of 0.92.

explain.text: At 5.2 the slope is 1.22 in units of $10^{-4}$: every gradient through this unit is cut ten-thousandfold. Scaling the income first is the fix.

ideas: The backward pass multiplies by every layer's activation slope. The sigmoid's is at most 0.25, so ten layers can cost a factor of $9.5 \times 10^{-7}$.
A saturated unit sits where the curve is flat: tanh's slope at 3 is 0.0099. Unscaled inputs saturate the first layer.
ReLU passes a gradient unchanged on its positive side, but a unit that is never on is dead and never learns.
summary.trap: A stuck training loss is a failure to fit, not overfitting: check the gradients before the data.

quiz.prose: A gradient crosses six sigmoid layers, each at its steepest point.
quiz.question: What factor do the slopes apply? Give it in units of $10^{-4}$, to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Raise 0.25 to the sixth power.

byKey.linear: You multiplied by 6 instead of raising to the sixth.

quiz.question: Why does a ReLU stack not shrink a gradient the way a sigmoid stack does?

options.text: Its slope is exactly 1 wherever the unit is on
Its slope is 0 everywhere, so nothing passes
options.why: Its slope is 1 for positive inputs; 0 only where the unit is off.

options.text: Its slope is 0.25 like the sigmoid's, but it is faster
options.why: The slope is 1 on the positive side, not 0.25.

options.text: It has no slope at all
options.why: ReLU has slope 1 or 0 almost everywhere.

feedback.correct: Slope 1 on the positive side passes the gradient unchanged.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What is ReLU's slope for $z > 0$?

explain.text: ReLU is $\max(0, z)$, so its slope is 1 for $z > 0$: a live path keeps its gradient. The risk is dead units, with slope 0 on every row.

quiz.prose: Unscaled features near 1,000 enter a tanh layer whose weights have sd 0.1.
quiz.question: What happens in the first layer?

options.text: The units saturate and pass almost no gradient
Nothing: the weights are small, so the layer is fine
options.why: Weights of 0.1 times inputs of 1,000 give pre-activations near 100.

options.text: The units die, as ReLU units do
options.why: tanh units do not die; they saturate, with slopes near 0 but never exactly 0.

options.text: Only the last layer is affected
options.why: The first layer sees the raw inputs, so it saturates first.

feedback.correct: Saturation from the first layer: $|z|$ near 100 gives a slope near 0.

explain.text: A weight of 0.1 on an input of 1,000 already gives 100. At $|z| = 100$, $1 - \tanh^2$ is 0 to machine precision, so nothing flows back.
